units.title: The art of the told story
Tell it in the real world

lessons.title: Pick one small moment
lessons.tip: A good story is often one small moment, not a whole life. Choose a moment when something changed: a surprise, a mistake, a first time. Ask: What happened? Why did it matter? What did I learn or feel? A true, small moment beats a long list of events.
sources: Aesop’s fables and the Brothers Grimm (public domain): classic story shapes, retold in original wording
Common oral-storytelling teaching: story arc, stakes, hook and landing (concepts only)

lessons.title: Want, obstacle, change
lessons.tip: Most stories have an arc: a person wants something, something gets in the way, they try, and something changes. Add stakes: what could be lost? Without stakes, there is no reason to care. Tell what happens in order, and make each step cause the next.
sources: Aesop’s fables and the Brothers Grimm (public domain): classic story shapes, retold in original wording
Common oral-storytelling teaching: story arc, stakes, hook and landing (concepts only)

lessons.title: Details that make it real
lessons.tip: Details make a story real: a name, a place, a sound, a number. “My uncle’s green van with the broken door” is better than “a vehicle.” But keep only the details that help the story, and let one or two strong details do the work.
sources: Aesop’s fables and the Brothers Grimm (public domain): classic story shapes, retold in original wording
Common oral-storytelling teaching: story arc, stakes, hook and landing (concepts only)

lessons.title: Hook and landing
lessons.tip: Open with a hook: a surprising line, a strong image or a question. Then land the ending: return to your opening image or finish with the change. Don’t end with “and that’s my story.” Pause, say your last line, and stop.
sources: Aesop’s fables and the Brothers Grimm (public domain): classic story shapes, retold in original wording
Common oral-storytelling teaching: story arc, stakes, hook and landing (concepts only)

lessons.title: Voice, pace and pauses
lessons.tip: In storytelling your voice carries the story. Slow down for important moments, speed up a little for action, lower your voice for secrets, and pause before a surprise. Silence is a tool. Practice by telling the story aloud, not by reading it silently.
sources: Aesop’s fables and the Brothers Grimm (public domain): classic story shapes, retold in original wording
Common oral-storytelling teaching: story arc, stakes, hook and landing (concepts only)

lessons.title: Bring people to life
lessons.tip: When you retell what someone said, give them a voice: a different pace, pitch or word. Say, “My mother looked at me and said, ‘You are late again.’” Keep it brief. Use “said,” and show the person with a gesture or a face, not a long imitation.

Common oral-storytelling teaching: story arc, stakes, hook and landing (concepts only)

lessons.title: Read your listeners
lessons.tip: A story is shared with listeners. Look at them, watch their faces and adjust: if they look lost, slow down; if they laugh, wait for the laugh to finish; if they lean in, keep going. You can ask a short question. Start where they are, not where you are.
sources: Aesop’s fables and the Brothers Grimm (public domain): classic story shapes, retold in original wording
Common oral-storytelling teaching: story arc, stakes, hook and landing (concepts only)

lessons.title: Trim and practice
lessons.tip: Most first drafts are too long. Cut what does not move the story: repeated details, side trips, long explanations. Aim for two minutes, about 250 to 300 words. Tell it aloud, time it and trim again. Keep the hook, the turning point and the landing.
sources: Aesop’s fables and the Brothers Grimm (public domain): classic story shapes, retold in original wording
Common oral-storytelling teaching: story arc, stakes, hook and landing (concepts only)

lessons.title: And, but, therefore
lessons.tip: Many good stories move on three small words. “And” sets the scene. “But” brings the problem. “Therefore” shows what happens because of it. “Rita lost the watch, but no one had seen it, therefore she searched every stall.” If your story only uses “and then,” it is a list. Look for the “but” and the “therefore” and put them early.
sources: Oral-storytelling traditions and public-domain folktale collections (structure ideas only; no text copied)
Common storytelling-workshop practice: and, but, therefore; setup and payoff; time-boxed tellings (original wording)

lessons.title: Show character through choices
lessons.tip: We learn who a person is by what they choose when it costs them something. A kind person might give up their seat; a stubborn person might refuse help. Let the character make a hard choice in your story, and show it with an action, not a label. “She handed him her umbrella and walked on in the rain” says more than “She was kind.”
sources: Oral-storytelling traditions and public-domain folktale collections (structure ideas only; no text copied)
Common storytelling-workshop practice: and, but, therefore; setup and payoff; time-boxed tellings (original wording)

lessons.title: Details for the ear
lessons.tip: Listeners cannot see the page, so they need to see the scene in their minds. Use details from the senses: what the place smelled like, the sound of a door, the feel of a cold handle. Pick two or three details, not twenty. Name them in simple words. A concrete detail makes a listener say, “I know that place.”

lessons.title: Setup, surprise and payoff
lessons.tip: Humor and surprise work in three steps. The setup creates an expectation. The surprise breaks it. The payoff is the moment people laugh or gasp. Plant a small detail early and bring it back later: “the red umbrella” can return at the end. Keep jokes short, and leave a tiny pause before the surprise. If the audience does not react, keep going calmly.
sources: Oral-storytelling traditions and public-domain folktale collections (structure ideas only; no text copied)
Common storytelling-workshop practice: and, but, therefore; setup and payoff; time-boxed tellings (original wording)

lessons.title: Layered tellings
lessons.tip: Experienced tellers often tell two stories at once: the surface events and a deeper meaning underneath. A story about repairing a boat can also be about forgiveness. Use a frame, such as returning to one object at the start and end, to unify the telling. Trust the audience to feel the second layer.

lessons.title: Restraint and implication
lessons.tip: The strongest moments are often the quietest. Instead of saying that your father was afraid, show what he did: he read the letter twice and went out to fix a gate that was not broken. Stop at the moment of greatest tension; silence is part of the telling.

lessons.title: Shape a true story
lessons.tip: Personal stories are not simply what happened; you choose what to tell. Pick one change, such as the moment you stopped lying. If real people appear, consider how they would feel hearing it.

lessons.title: Body, space and presence
lessons.tip: Your body tells the story too. Use space: give each character or place a spot on the stage and return to it, so the audience always knows who is speaking. lessons.title: Respond to a live audience
lessons.tip: A told story is a conversation with the audience. Watch for signals: leaning in means you have them; checking phones means you are losing them. Adjust your pace, shorten a detour or add a vivid detail. If something unexpected happens, such as a noise, acknowledge it briefly and return to the story. Keep an extra short ending ready for when time runs out. Leave a little space for laughter, and wait until it fades before continuing.

lessons.title: Retell and adapt traditional tales
lessons.tip: Traditional tales belong to communities. You can retell them, but tell them with care. Keep the tale’s core: what it is about and what changes. Adapt the setting, the characters and the language so they speak to your audience: a fox and a crow can become a manager and a new employee. Credit the source when you know it, and avoid presenting a sacred or culturally restricted story as your own entertainment without permission. Say what is yours and what is the tradition’s.

lessons.title: Whose story is it?
lessons.tip: Stories involve people. Before you tell a story with real people in it, ask: Is it mine to tell? Would they be hurt or exposed? Can I change names and identifying details? When the story is about someone else’s pain, let them speak for themselves where possible, or ask for their consent. Avoid stereotypes: give characters from other cultures the same depth you give your own. Tell stories that leave people with dignity.
